newsitem.title: UK: Ex-Premier Heath dismisses Major's Labour attacks.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Premier Heath dismisses Major's Labour attacks.

text.p: A former Conservative prime minister on Sunday dramatically undermined election year efforts by incumbent John Major to brand the opposition Labour party as a threat to Britain's economy and national unity.

In a television interview, Edward Heath, who was prime minister from 1970 to 1974 and is still a member of parliament, said there was "no danger" that Britain would split apart, as Major has suggested, if Labour honoured a pledge to give Scotland its own parliament.

He also dismissed claims by Conservative cabinet ministers that half a million jobs could be lost if Labour introduced a statutory minimum wage, saying: "I'm not sure how strongly members of the government think that's right."
The interview by Heath, 80, marked the second time in a week that he has embarrassed Major in the run-up to a general election widely expected to be held on May 1.
On Thursday, he launched an attack on Major for his lack of leadership with regard to the European Union and warned that the Conservatives could split apart over the issue after the election.

The Conservatives, running about 18 percentage points behind Labour in public opinion polls, have been campaigning for weeks to convince voters that they would be taking a risk by putting the first Labour government into power since 1979.

A massive poster campaign has been launched under the slogan "New Labour, New Danger", and on Thursday Major opened a parliamentary debate on Labour's plans for constitutional change, an issue he believes will be a key one at the election.

But Heath told BBC television that if he had been returned to power at an election in 1974 which Labour narrowly won, he would have set up an assembly in Edinburgh to give Scotland greater control over its own affairs.

Dismissing Major's warnings about "devolution" of power, Heath said Britain gave federal systems to Canada, Australia, South Africa, and its former colonies in central Africa, and, as one of the Allied victors in World War Two, to Germany.
"You cannot say that any of those have broken up. When you look at Germany, it is the most successful development since the Second World War," he said.
"It (devolution) has no danger to the unity of the United Kingdom, none whatever."
Heath said a minimum wage was a valuable tool in preventing exploitation of workers provided it was set at the right level.

He noted that for certain industries such as agriculture, minimum wages had been fixed as long ago as in 1909, when they were introduced by Winston Churchill, then a Liberal minister, but later a Conservative prime minister and World War Two leader of a government of national unity.
The purpose of the minimum wage is to avoid sweated labour, and quite rightly so," he said. "There are now elements (in Britain's labour force) that have got very low wages indeed."
